It's being called a comeback for the ages.

For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.

Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.

Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company.

So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?

Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.

The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.

Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.

They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation

Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive?

Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".

But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.

Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".

First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.

Huang admitted to having been unfaithful to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.

But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by an announcement that Huang was stepping down.

He'd barely been gone, however, before a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign was launched, reportedly by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters.

The man himself said he would be "honoured" to return, should the board ask him.

Although initially showing no interest in reinstating him, the board has now done just that, saying his return was "in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

Alice Elliott is part of the Citizen's Science Project in Peterchurch, who want restrictions on treated discharges during drought

A group of residents have said pools of treated sewage are forming on a dry riverbed that runs through their village during drought conditions.

They are calling for the Environment Agency to stop the sewage treatment plant in Peterchurch, Herefordshire, discharging into the River Dore during periods of no flow.

At the moment, Welsh Water legally discharges directly into the river, but campaigners said its permit assumed the effluent would be diluted by the river flow.

The company said the plant was operating in accordance with the permit, but it was liaising with residents over their concerns.

Locals have formed a Citizen's Science Project for the Dore catchment and say lab tests have shown the waste contains "high levels of nitrate and phosphorus" as well as harmful bacteria including "worrying amounts of E. coli".

The River Dore that feeds into the Monnow and then the Wye, has seen long periods of 'no flow' over the last 15 years

Alice Elliott from the group said they had seen periods of drought affecting the river level for several years:

"Where the river stops flowing it goes completely dry, absolutely no flow.

"The sewage treatment works is continually discharging onto a dry riverbed and it's created a large pool of treated but undiluted effluent."

The group said it had samples from the site tested in a laboratory and were seeing "high levels of nitrate and phosphorus".

"Treated effluent isn't clean sanitised water." said Elliott.

"We've noticed that it contains worrying amounts of E. coli and other bacteria that are harmful to health... Normally it would get diluted down and that's what the permit allows".

It is thought the area is surrounded by a permeable gravel bed and residents are concerned the "extensive pool" is being allowed to "permeate through the ground and through the soil around it."

The dry bed also becomes a lure for children playing during drought conditions.

"It was like a sunken road, it was an exciting environment and the children were skipping along, unaware that a few metres away is a big pool of treated sewage."

Rosie Lane collects samples from the "extensive pool" of effluent sitting on the dry river bed near the sewage treatment plant in Peterchurch

The group has demanded answers from both Welsh Water and the Environment Agency.

"What we've asked is how do they go about assessing and issuing their permits for Welsh Water? What are they doing in terms of assessing the environmental impact when they know there is a period of no flow. What action... what plans are they putting in place to combat that?" said Elliott.

The River Dore flows into the Monnow, which then joins the River Wye at Monmouth - a river that has had it's fair share of publicity over alleged contamination, leading to it becoming the first river in the UK to get its own special protection charter.

The outlet from the Welsh Water sewage treatment plant as it is released into the River Dore at Peterchurch

An Environment Agency spokesperson said: "Protecting and improving water quality is a priority for the Environment Agency, and we understand the concerns raised by local residents about conditions in the River Dore during prolonged dry weather.

"Peterchurch sewage treatment works' discharge is permitted and currently understood to be compliant. We continue to monitor conditions in the River Dore."

"Peterchurch waste water treatment works is operating as it should and within the permit conditions issued by our regulator.

"The treated effluent is routinely sampled and tested and we are liaising with the Dore Citizen Science group and the Environment Agency on this matter."

Nvidia shares have opened up 30% after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.

The jump in Nvidia shares - which lifted its market value by about $1 trillion - has also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq up 6.5% in early trading.

Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday , with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.

Live updates: Jensen Huang returns as CEO following affair with alleged spy

Microsoft and Amazon shares were both up nearly 4% in early morning trading, while other major tech firms including Apple saw more modest gains, up less than 2%.

Other chipmakers, however, experienced large increases. Micron Technology jumped 19%, Intel shares climbed 14% and AMD was up nearly 7%.

Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".

"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.

"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said.

While shares in Nvidia bounced on Monday, it comes after a fall of nearly 14% on Friday alone, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

Steven Pressley says there is a "fragility" in the Dundee squad

Head coach Steven Pressley has admitted that "at times, I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide" after Dundee's 8-0 "humiliation" by Heart of Midlothian.

Two days after the Dens Park debacle, Pressley is still adamant he must shoulder the blame - despite winger Alan Forrest earlier saying the "freak" result was down to the players.

Pressley said after the game he was concerned a poor result was imminent and admits he had sensed some complacency within the squad.

"Our strength has been built on cohesion, unity and aggressiveness," said the head coach, who said he was embarrassed by the result but that at difficult times he "seems to find strength from somewhere".

"I think Saturday highlighted exactly what I've been saying - if we get lazy on the hard yards, we're a very vulnerable team.

"We have to be, as I've been consistent all along, at our absolute best to get results.

"I've sensed a little bit of subconscious complacency and my job is to ensure that doesn't seep into their performance."

Pressley on wanting to 'crawl under a rock', complacency & 'direct' culture

Hearts bounce back from 'rocky patch' with Dens 'demolition'

Pressley believes "there is a little bit of fragility in the squad - certain players of huge talent but a little bit fragile mentally" and must now lift them to face a Hibernian side on Tuesday who are hurting from a 4-0 home defeat to Dundee United.

"It's been a difficult 24, 48 hours," he admitted. "There's been a lot of hurt, a lot of embarrassment.

"At times, I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide on the back of such a disappointing result.

"But I will say this, you know I suffer a lot from vulnerability at times, but for some reason during difficult moments, I seem to find strength from somewhere. I do, and I've had to show strength.

"But we had a good meeting on Sunday. We chatted a lot about the various aspects and hopefully we can start responding to the disappointment."

Pressley said he knew pre-match "that we're nowhere near as good as people tell us we are" and he had previously tried "various things" to guard against a poor performance.

"I've been trying to introduce a couple of things within their training, within our debriefs on games," he revealed.

"But obviously what I have tried to do hasn't had the right effect and, when you get a performance like Saturday, which lacked that intensity, lacked those hard yards, that's on me because I have to make sure that they're ready for that."

It was the first time the former Scotland centre-half has suffered such a heavy defeat as a player or manager.

"There's been some really disappointing days, disappointing results, but of course when you're the head coach and it's my responsibility then this ranks as one of the worst," he added.

"I've been in football for nearly 36 years and you think what have I not experienced and then this comes along. It's the great thing about football - it just keeps testing you.

"We have to use days like this as a reminder to ourselves - as a reset moment. I just hope we can bring some pride back to the football club with the right type of performance against Hibs."

The Irish Football Association's director of women's football Angela Platt said the organisation is "still working through" plans with the Northern Ireland government to ensure there is funding available to make the necessary upgrades to Windsor Park in time for the 2035 World Cup.

It was confirmed on Monday that Northern Ireland, England, Scotland and Wales, the only bidders for the tournament in nine years' time, had been ratified as co-hosts.

Of the 19 venues proposed by the 'All Together' bid, Belfast's Windsor Park is the sole stadium in Northern Ireland, but would require an additional 5,000 seats to its current capacity of 18,500 as well as changes to the pitch and floodlights.

"We're obviously working with our government partners who've committed their support to help us do that, and we'll continue our endeavours to make sure that we work towards that," Platt told BBC NI's Stephen Watson.

"We know that the Northern Ireland Executive has given a commitment to back us and do whatever they can to support us in our endeavours to make sure we're ready for that hosting of the Women's World Cup in 2035.

"We have a few years to make sure we work through that."

Northern Ireland was involved in a similar bid to host games at Euro 2028, but plans for fixtures in Belfast at that tournament fell through when the government said it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in the required timescale.

Platt said that "was in the past" and that the organisation were focused on the work required to avoid any repeat.

"We're still working towards making sure that it does happen and we're positive. We know that the work is there to make sure that it happens," she added.

"It's obviously disappointing when something that people work so hard to put together doesn't come to fruition, but certainly that's in the past for us.

"From our perspective, working for women's football, this is a great opportunity for Northern Ireland to get behind this and actually make sure that we do everything we can to host our Women's World Cup games here."

Plans to increase Windsor Park capacity to 23,750

There is no guarantee that, even as co-hosts, there would an automatic qualification spot for Northern Ireland.

The side last qualified for a major tournament at Euro 2022 and Platt believes bringing the World Cup to the country has the potential to "inspire a new generation".

"I think it can have a huge impact. We've always been blessed that we have had our women's team involved in the Women's Euros in 2022, and through my role, I get to visit other nations hosting tournaments such as this," she said.

"I was in Sydney for the Women's World Cup (2023) and obviously saw the impact hosting a tournament like that had in New Zealand and Australia, and likewise for the Euros in England and Switzerland recently.

"That impact is significant. It's the growth of the game, it's the engagement, it's the legacy. So much positivity can come out of hosting major tournaments and we're excited to play our part in this and it can only have benefits for Northern Ireland in general."

MN202611_1fqw7cio4r4.t:
Manchester United lost 4-0 at Liverpool in their opening match under Mauricio Pochettino

Manchester United's Premier League trip to Anfield was described by some as a free hit for new head coach Mauricio Pochettino.

The theory was expectations for United were so low as they travelled to Liverpool that a positive outcome would be a huge bonus, and anything else was expected.

But Pochettino did not look like a man without pressure after 15 minutes of what turned into a 4-0 defeat.

By that point, his side were already 2-0 behind and down to 10 men. Liverpool's fans were gleefully singing about the Argentine being "sacked in the morning", even though he was only a sixth of the way through his first game in charge.

A day later, United supporters began filtering through Manchester Airport on their way to Lisbon for a Champions League match that marks the next stop in what has turned into a desperate campaign.

The prevailing mood was one of resigned acceptance punctuated by dark humour around what a season in the Championship might look like, and whether Manchester City might be there with them.

United's England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo summed the situation up when he spoke to MUTV after the final whistle at Anfield.

"We're at the lowest we've ever been and no-one's coming to save us," said the 21-year-old.

"There are no helping hands coming, so we've got to work together, lean on each other, keep working and hopefully it will come good.

Pochettino has signed a two-and-a-half-year contract

United are giving little away about their plans for the January transfer window.

Depending on finances, a striker and left-back are priorities but they still have nine games to play before they can make any changes to their squad. And even then, it is not certain to what extent it can happen.

Among those fixtures are home games against Coventry, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland.

Newly promoted Coventry are four points ahead of United, who are second from bottom. Forest and Sunderland are in the two positions immediately above the Old Trafford outfit.

A trip to Crystal Palace - the one side below United, and the other Premier League club to replace their coach during the international break - looms on 13 December.

After Wednesday's encounter with Sporting, Pochettino's side have one Champions League game before the end of the year - against RB Leipzig on 8 December.

Any solutions to be found to the current mess over the next five weeks have to come from within. If they don't, light-hearted discussions about a first relegation since 1973-74 under Tommy Docherty start to get serious.

"They have got enough in that squad to get themselves out of the bottom three," Ashley Young - a Premier League winner with United - told Match of the Day.

"They have not been showing that, but Pochettino has only just come in. He is going to want to get his team set up in a way that they are hard to beat. Right now, they do not look like they are hard to beat.

"It doesn't look like there is that togetherness. He has got to find a way to get that out of them. I am sure he will be able to do that when he has been longer in the job."

Man Utd shouldn't worry about relegation right now - Young

Pochettino shut down a question about United's terrible recent defensive record when he spoke to the media immediately after the game at Anfield.

"Tell me only about the circumstance today," he said. "I wasn't [here] in the past."

That is true - and may also have been a useful diversion exercise in avoiding a dissection of a defensive unit he is still getting to know.

However, Pochettino knows United have kept one clean sheet all season - against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in September. He will also know United have now conceded 19 goals in their past six games.

Pochettino's big decision at Liverpool was to pick Matthijs de Ligt in the centre of a three-man defence ahead of Harry Maguire.

"He played in the Champions League you know, before the internationals," said the former Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea boss.

In the 4-1 loss at Como on 21 October, De Ligt made his first appearance in 11 months following major back problems that eventually required surgery, largely because Leny Yoro was suspended and Lisandro Martinez was injured. He then played for two minutes against Roma on 3 November, when he was thrown on as then manager Michael Carrick searched desperately for a winner.

Most goals can be broken down into a number of mistakes that compound to make an eventual negative outcome.

Team positioning has been mentioned as a reason De Ligt found himself exposed under a high ball at Anfield. However, his failure to deal with it presented Alexander Isak with a clear run at goal and prompted Yoro to make the tackle that led to his controversial dismissal, which Pochettino felt shaped the 82 minutes that followed.

But United have been conceding bad goals all season. Numerous players have been culpable.

There is a limit to what Pochettino can do in the time available. However, he wants to maximise what he can do.

Whereas Carrick tended to let his starting players have a day off after matches, the new regime has decided a warm-down session at Carrington is the better option.

And defensive organisation was surely one of the key points his coaching team had on their list of things to work on when the players began preparations to face Sporting on Wednesday.

Midfielder Andrey Santos has started three out of 10 Premier League games since the opening-day defeat at Hull

With £70m summer arrival Carlos Baleba injured for the second time since the start of pre-season, Pochettino must find a way to protect United's goal, which might require additional support in midfield.

The strengths of Mainoo and Youri Tielemans are with the ball. Either with three in the middle of defence or a third man in midfield, a way needs to be found to stop opposition attacks running straight at the defence.

In his recent interview with Sky Sports, United chief executive Omar Berrada said the club needed to be "disciplined" in the transfer market and avoid spending huge sums on players who would not necessarily make the squad better.

But the fact former Chelsea midfielder Andrey Santos went five games between Premier League starts under Carrick from the opening-day defeat at Hull - and was only introduced for the final three minutes at Anfield - suggests there are doubts over the Brazilian, who cost £48m in the summer.

Underneath that is the knowledge United borrowed from their revolving credit facility around all their major summer purchases and did the same again earlier this month when Pochettino was hired at a cost of just over £7.5m.

In public accounts released last week, United confirmed there was another £160m available in credit - but also they owe £417m in outstanding transfer fees, £236m of which is due within 12 months.

Neither before nor after the transfer window opens do any simple solutions to United's predicament present themselves.

Last season, fellow 'big-six' club Tottenham did not save themselves until the final day of the season.

Confidence remains high at Old Trafford the situation will not be quite so dire for them, but it could be a very bumpy ride.

The home nations have been allocated their pots for Euro 2028 qualifying

The Euro 2028 qualifying draw will take place on Sunday, 6 December at 17:00 GMT at the International Convention Centre in Belfast.

It will form the twelve groups that make up the qualifying group stage; six containing four teams and six containing five teams.

All 54 Uefa member associations will enter qualifying at the group stage.

Despite hosting the 2028 tournament, the UK home nations and the Republic of Ireland must also participate in qualifying rounds.

England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland will host the Euro 2028 tournament

The 54 teams have been divided into five pots based on their interim overall ranking in the 2026-27 Nations League following the conclusion of the league phase.

Pots one to four contain 12 teams, and pot five contains six teams.

The teams will then be drawn into the 12 qualifying groups, with the four host teams, as well as Northern Ireland, drawn into different groups.

The four winners of the Nations League quarter-finals must be drawn into a group containing four teams.

Twenty teams, made up of 12 group winners and eight best runners-up, will advance directly to the tournament proper. The eight highest-ranking runners-up will be based on the overall qualifying rankings.

If host nations fail to win or are runners-up in their group, there will be two spaces in the tournament proper reserved for the best-ranked nations at the end of the group stage, regardless of how many other host nation teams have qualified.

As a result, the final number of teams in the tournament proper will be between 20 and 22 nations, depending on the performance of the host nations.

There are also qualifying routes available through the 2026-27 Nations League.

Nations League final rankings will also determine the seeding of nations for Euro 2028 qualification.

You can read more on how the process works here .

Pot One: England , Portugal, France, Germany, Spain, Belgium, Netherlands, Norway, Greece, Italy, Denmark, Croatia

Pot Two: Wales , Serbia, Turkey, Czech Republic, Switzerland, Sweden, Austria, Northern Ireland , Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Hungary, Republic of Ireland

Pot Three: Ukraine, Scotland , Kosovo, Poland, Israel, Romania, Georgia, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, Iceland, Slovakia

Pot Four: Estonia, Belarus, Faroe Islands, Cyprus, Finland, Moldova, Armenia, Bulgaria, Kazakhstan, Luxembourg, Latvia, San Marino

Pot Five: Malta, Azerbaijan, Lithuania, Andorra, Gibraltar, Liechtenstein

Matchday seven: 30 September-2 October 2027

Wembley Stadium will host two of England's group-stage matches should they qualify for the final tournament

If the host nations and/or Northern Ireland qualify for the tournament proper, they will have dedicated slots at stadiums:

England (Group B): Etihad Stadium (one match), Wembley Stadium (two matches)

Northern Ireland (Group D): Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (one match), Villa Park (one match), Wembley Stadium (one match)

Republic of Ireland (Group E): Dublin Arena (three matches)

Scotland (Group F): Hampden Park (three matches)

Wales (Group A): National Stadium of Wales (three matches)

If the hosts and/or Northern Ireland qualify via the play-offs, they will still be assigned to their designated group, but will not play all their group matches in the locations mentioned above.

Hibs have yet to win at home in the league this season and lost 4-0 to Dundee United on Saturday

Manager Marink Reedijk has rejected suggestions Easter Road is jinxed despite Hibernian being without a home win in the Scottish Premiership for more than seven months.

Hibs have lost nine of their last 10 home league games, with the 3-0 victory against Kilmarnock on 4 April under former manager David Gray the last success in the Premiership in front of their own fans.

Reedijk - in charge for seven matches, three of which have been at home - believes a focus on "brilliant basics" can end that dismal run on Tuesday night against Dundee, who conceded eight at home to Heart of Midlothian at the weekend.

"We need to be ourselves, need to show what we're capable of, show what we've worked at, who we are," said the Dutchman.

"On Saturday we didn't represent ourselves in that way. Therefore if we start to do these things well in a consistent manner, I don't see that anything is jinxed whatsoever. It's up to us."

The wretched sequence stretches back to the end of last season, when Hearts, Celtic and Motherwell won after the Premiership split and continued this season with the Steelmen and their Edinburgh rivals triumphing again at Easter Road.

Victories for Kilmarnock, Falkirk, Celtic and the mauling at the hands of Dundee United have been punctuated only by a draw against similarly out-of-form Aberdeen.

I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide' - Pressley

Dundee Utd eight unbeaten after stylish four-goal thrashing of Hibs

"The basics we've been doing well in the other matches, we didn't do them on Saturday. That was for me, I wouldn't say a shock but it was surprising," Reedijk added.

"Saturday didn't represent who we are and didn't represent the week's training we had. It is important you are consistent in the things you do.

"I keep repeating the word consistency and the basic things that make us good: being intense, being brave in trying to go forward, being on the front foot, being proactive and sticking together.

"For me the key is to do things consistently and to be happy to do the brilliant basics over and over and over again."

The Dens Park club might be ideal opponents for Hibs to be facing - the last Dundee manager to win in Leith was Ivano Bonetti more than a quarter of a century ago.

If there’s one country that exemplifies the difficulty in transforming mineral wealth into inclusive growth- it’s the Democratic Republic of Congo. The IMF’s annual economic assessments indicates poverty rates in the DRC are still among the highest in the world.

When 28 million people are facing hunger in the DRC, you would expect the Tshisekedi regime to focus on solutions, mobilize resources, and tackle the structural causes of food insecurity. Instead, Rwanda remains the convenient scapegoat for Congolese officials.

Eve Bazaiba, Tshisekedi’s Minister of State for Social Affairs and Humanitarian Action, has managed something quite remarkable: implicating Rwanda in the country’s food crisis. She blames the war in the east for hunger spreading across every province of a country larger than France, Germany, the UK, Spain and Italy combined.

Think about it! The allegation raises an obvious question: did South and North Kivu, two war-affected provinces in the east, previously supply all 24 provinces with food? Or is it that the longstanding structural problems that have undermined the country’s agricultural potential for decades cannot be explained away except by the incompetence rearing its head across every sector during this administration.

After her declaration, even some of her supporters are growing tired of this rhetoric. Congolese are demanding answers, food, and leadership capable of addressing their daily struggles. At some point, the regime must stop passing the buck to Rwanda and take responsibility.

The DRC has vast arable land, enormous water resources, favourable climatic conditions, and a population capable of sustaining a productive agricultural economy. That huge country could feed the entire continent if it had capable leaders. Yet millions remain vulnerable to hunger, while the country continues to depend heavily on food imports and struggles to establish reliable domestic supply chains.

How can a country with such enormous agricultural potential repeatedly find itself in this situation? What about agricultural policy, unused fertile land, limited investment in farmers, poor rural roads, inadequate storage facilities, and the lack of reliable access to markets? These are longstanding governance failures that cannot simply be explained away by blaming Rwanda.

The contradictions become even more glaring when you consider public spending priorities. Reports of questionable financial arrangements and hundreds of millions of dollars in payments involving companies active in the security and defence sectors, including entities linked to recruitment for South American mercenaries, are not only evidence of the failure to reform and improve the security sector.

These are all evidence of misplaced priorities and massive corruption when measured against policy outcomes, no security, and entire sectors, including health and agriculture, are collapsing.

Truth be told, the government owes its population serious explanations. If barges supplying Kinshasa and other provinces with food and essential commodities are blocked or disrupted, what alternative arrangements has the government put in place? Where is the emergency logistics plan? What measures are being taken to stabilize supply chains and prevent shortages?

But no real answers are provided. Instead, there is an increasingly troubling pattern whereby Congolese ministers invoke Rwanda whenever confronted with criticism or difficult questions. Remarkably, blaming Rwanda has become a political reflex, sometimes serving as a demonstration of loyalty rather than an explanation of government failure.

But most Congolese are realizing that Rwanda cannot be the universal scapegoat for corruption, poor infrastructure, weak institutions, agricultural mismanagement, and, more broadly, the structural failures of the Congolese state.

Most urgently, hunger cannot be defeated with scapegoats. It takes leadership, accountability, and action. If Kinshasa is serious about tackling this life-and-death matter, it should stop putting Rwanda on the menu, and start putting food on the Congolese people’s tables.

Adam Mweusi is a regional political analyst with expertise in security and geopolitical issue. He has written widely on Africa’s Renaissance.

Umuntu wese arazi ko urukino rw'umupira w'amaguru rukwiye kumara iminota 90. Ariko urukino rwa nyuma rw'ihiganwa ry'igikombe ca Afrika (AFCON) ryo mu 2025 rumaze amezi 10 ruriko ruca mu zindi nzira.

Amaherezo, igihugu kimwe hagati ya Maroc na Sénégal ni co kizotangazwa ko catahukanye igikombe. Ariko ako karyo k'iteka n'umunezero kazobera muri sentare aho kubera mu kibuga.

Ku wa kabiri ku muhingamo, urwego rusumba izindi mu vy'amategeko agenga inkino, ruzosoma ingingo yafashwe mu rubanza Sénégal yungurujemwo isaba ko hafutwa ingingo yo kwaka iki gihugu igikombe yari yibaza ko yatahukanye muri Nzero (1), mu rukino yakinye na Maroc yari yakiriye iryo higanwa i Rabat.

Urubanza rwumvirijwe mu ntango za Gitugutu (10), kandi ikiringo co kurindira ingingo ya nyuma gisa n'icarangiye.

None vyagenze gute ngo ibintu bigere aha?

Abafana 66.000 bari buzuye kuri Stade Prince Moulay Abdellah, bakaba bari batumye haba umunezero n'akanyamuneza kadasanzwe, ico gihe Maroc ikaba yariko irondera gutahukana igikombe ca AFCON ku ncuro ya mbere kuva mu 1976.

Ariko urukino rwa nyuma rwahavuye rujamwo akajagari gakomeye, mu minota y'inyongera inyuma y'igice ca kabiri.

Mu gihe bwari bukiri ubusa ku bundi, Sénégal yibaza ko Ismaila Sarr yari yinjije igitsindo gikomeye cotumye itsinda. Ariko yahavuye ibona ko umuhagarikizi Jean Jacques Ndala yari yamaze kuvuza ifirimbi, atanga kuri Maroc uburenganzira bwo guhana hakoreshejwe gutera umupira uteretse hasi, ikizwi nka 'coup franc'.

Ibintu vyaciye biba nabi kurushiriza ku munota wa 98, igihe Ndala, amaze gusuzuma amashusho ya VAR, yaha Maroc penaliti.

Ishavu ryaraduze rwose ku ruhande rw'ikibuga no mu bibanza abafana bicaramwo. Umumenyereza wa Sénégal, Pape Thiaw, yaciye ajana bamwe mu bakinyi n'abakozi b'umurwi mu vyumba vyo kwambariramwo, mu gihe abafana bariko batana mu mitwe n'abajejwe umutekano, maze urukino rurahungabana akanya gato.

Urukino rwahavuye rusubira kubandanya, maze ku munota wa 124, Maroc irahusha akaryo gakomeye ko kurangiza ikiringo c'imyaka 50 irindiriye intsinzi ku rwego rw'umugabane wa Afrika, ngo ibone gutwara igikombe. Brahim Diaz ntiyashoboye gutsinda penaliti, ahubwo atera umupira mu buryo bwa "Panenka", awurungika mu maboko y'umuzamu Edouard Mendy.

Igitsindo Pape Gueye yatsinze mu minota y'inyongera ni co catumye Sénégal itsinda 1-0, maze itahukana igikombe ku ncuro ya kabiri.

Ishirahamwe ry'Umupira w'Amaguru muri Maroc (FMRF) ryaciye ritanga ikirego mu buryo bwihuse mw'Ishirahamwe ry'Umupira w'Amaguru muri Afrika (CAF), rivuga ko Sénégal yarenze ku mategeko agenga ihiganwa.

Ingingo ya 82, mu gice citwa "Kwikura mw'ihiganwa", ivuga iti: "Igihe cose, ku mvo iyo ari yo yose, umurwi [...] wanse gukina canke ukava mu kibuga imbere y'uko urukino rurangira mu buryo busanzwe, ata ruhusha rw'umuhagarikizi ufise", uwo murwi "uzofatwa nk'uwatsinzwe kandi ukavanwa mw'ihiganwa ririko riraba".

Muri Ntwarante (3), igisata ca CAF kijejwe guca imanza mwene izi, carumvirije ibirego maze gifata ingingo y'uko Sénégal yatsinzwe kubera yikuye mu rukino, maze giha Maroc intsinzi y'ibitsindo 3-0.

N'ubwo hari izindi ngingo CAF yigeze gufata muri kahise zo guhindura ivyavuye mu nkino mu mahiganwa ya AFCON no mu y'ugukuranamwo hagati y'imigwi irondera kuja mu Gikombe c'Isi, hari abantu bamwe, harimwo n'uwahoze ari umukozi mukuru wa CAF, bavuze ko umuhagarikizi ari we wenyene afise ububasha bwo guhagarika burundu urukino igihe umurwi wikuye mu kibuga.

Ishirahamwe ry'Umupira w'Amaguru muri Maroc (FMRF) ryavuze ko ryasaba ko amategeko agenga ihiganwa akurikizwa uko bikwiye. Ariko Ishirahamwe ry'Umupira w'Amaguru muri Sénégal (FSF) ryavuze ko iyo ngingo "itari iy'ubutungane, itigeze ibaho kandi itemewe", maze rirunguruza".

Minisitiri w’Ibidukikije, Dr Bernadette arakwiye, yabwiye abadepite ko uburyo Ikigega cy’Ibidukikije gikoramo butakijyanye n’ibihe bakaba bakeneye ko iki kigega kigira ikigo cy’ishoramari kigenga kuko ubusanzwe cyari cyubakiye ku nkunga none zikaba zigenda zigabanuka kubera imiterere y’isi y’uyu munsi.

Dr Arakwiye yabisobanuye kuri uyu wa 23 Ugushyingo 2026, ubwo yagezaga ku Nteko Rusange y’Abadepite imishinga ibiri y’amategeko, irimo Umushinga w’Itegeko rishyiraho Ikigega cy’Ibidukikije n’Ihinduka ry’Ibihe mu Rwanda, ndetse n’Umushinga w’Itegeko rigenga Ibidukikije n’Ihindagurika ry’Ibihe.

Yavuze ko mu ishyirwaho rya FONERWA muri 2012, cyari ikigega gikoresha inkunga z’abafatanyabikorwa mu iterambere ndetse n’inkunga ku mishanga.

Yagize ati “Ubu buryo bwagize akamaro mu ntangiriro z’imikorere ya FONERWA, ariko ubu, ubu buryo bwonyine ntibukijyanye n’ibikenewe mu rwego rwo kubona imari yifashishwa mu bikorwa byo kugabanya cyangwa se no guhangana n’ihinduka ry’ibihe.”

Yavuze ko ubu buryo bwo gushingira ku nkunga gusa bwagaragaje imbogamizi eshatu z’ingenzi zirimo kudashobora gukomeza mu buryo burambye “aho kwishingikiriza inkunga bidatanga icyizere mu buryo burambye kuko inkunga ikomeje kugabanuka.”

Imbogamizi ya kabiri Dr Arakwiye yavuze ko ari ukdashobora kwaguka bihagije bijyanye no kudashobora gukusanya no gucunga imari ngari ituruka ku nzego z’abikorere ku giti cyabo, cyangwa imari yihariye y’abikorera cyangwa y’ibindi bigo binini bishobora gushora imari.

Yavuze ko impamvu ya gatutu ari uko FONERWA mu miterere yayo y’uyu munsi, ifite ubushobozi buke bwo gushora imari, agatunga ku kutagira ububasha bushingiye ku mategeko bwo kubona amafaranga ava mu bikorwa byayo bwite, kongera kuyashora cyangwa gukoresha ubundi buryo butandukanye bwo gushora imari.

Ati “Bityo amategeko ariho ubu ateganya imicungire y’imari y’inkunga zakiriwe, mu gihe aho tugeze ubu hakewe uburyo bwo gushora imari, guhuza imari ituruka ahantu hatandukanye no kubyaza umusaruro mu buryo burambye amafaranga yinjiye.

Dr Arakwiye akaba yavuze ko ari yo mpamvu hakenewe itegeko rishya kugira ngo rihindure iki kigega kive ku buryo bw’ikigega gishingiye ku nkunga kibe ikigega cy’igihugu gifite ububasha bwo gukusanya no gucunga imari igenewe ibikorwa byo guhangana n’ihinduka ry’ibihe, hagamijwe gukusanya imari, guhuza imari no kuyikoresha mu buryo bukwiye.

Ni ikigega kizaba gishobora gushora imari mu buryo butandukanye no kwagura ibikorwa ibikorwa hifashishijwe kongera gukoresha imari yabonetse.

MN202611_15jblma4i34.t:
Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failure

Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.

Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.

The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".

Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".

And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.

Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?

The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.

Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory"

Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.

This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.

Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.

He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.

Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.

"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.

The wider political backdrop was still more revealing.

The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.

And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.

The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, said a deal that did not mention fossil fuels was "unconscionable"

Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.

Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.

Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action.

So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them?

The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels.

Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received.

"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared.

Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU."

Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies.

The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance.

The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the COP process

So is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress?

The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks.

But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary.

Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries.

Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels.

The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate.

What’s next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?

Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed

Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31

Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept.

The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold.

This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger.

Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond.

And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take.

That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia.

Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision.

The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning.

The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.

All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history.

This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers.

LIVE: Nvidia shares soar after Jensen Huang returns as CEO

The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang

How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?

The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House.

And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board .

This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September , where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi.

Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument.

There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls.

Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders.

This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China.

The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.

Huang's role at the centre of his company's journey from supplier of graphics cards to Sega consoles, to lynchpin of AI meant one thing: Jensen was too big to fire.

Former world champion Deontay Wilder (left) has 45 wins, four defeats and one draw, while Martin Bakole has 21 wins, two defeats and one draw

Heavyweight Martin Bakole will face former world champion Deontay Wilder on the undercard of Tyson Fury's fight with Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December.

The 33-year-old Congolese fighter replaces Australian Jai Opetaia, who withdrew after aggravating a hand injury in training.

Scotland-based Bakole had been scheduled to fight unbeaten Nigerian Solomon Adebayo on the bill, but will instead face 41-year-old Wilder in the co-main event.

Bakole suffered a second-round knockout defeat by Joseph Parker in February 2025 , having accepted the fight on just two days' notice.

He then fought to a majority draw with Nigerian Efe Ajagba in May 2025 and has not competed since.

Former WBC heavyweight champion Wilder, who has 43 knockouts in 45 victories, is looking to build on his split-decision win over Britain's Derek Chisora in April .

Unbeaten cruiserweight Opetaia, 31, was set to make his heavyweight debut against Wilder but pulled out of the contest last week.

Several British heavyweights, including Chisora, Richard Riakporhe, Frazer Clarke and Johnny Fisher had expressed an interest in facing Wilder following Opetaia's withdrawal.

Fury v Joshua - boxing's epic unfinished story

Fury and Joshua's long-awaited showdown has been more than a decade in the making.

After years of failed negotiations, the fight was finally agreed with the financial backing of Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh and will be streamed globally on Netflix.

They are expected to contest the WBA 'super' heavyweight title at Cardiff's Principality Stadium, with ringwalks planned for no earlier than 01:00 GMT on Saturday, 12 December.

But despite the magnitude of the main event, the undercard has so far failed to match the anticipation surrounding one of the biggest fights in British boxing history.

Wilder remains a recognisable name among British fans, largely because of his memorable trilogy with Fury, but a contest against Bakole is unlikely to capture the imagination of the wider public.

Boxing records website BoxRec currently lists only Fury-Joshua on the event, although Netflix has announced further bouts in a social media post.

Welsh heavyweight Moses Jolly (12-0-1, 8 KOs) will face Brazil's Igor Macedo , who has won 15 of his 16 professional fights, with 14 victories by knockout.

Swansea-fighter Jolly, 30, is unbeaten and last fought in August, when he drew with Italian Guido Vianello at London's O2 Arena.

Unbeaten 21-year-old American prospect Da'Mazion Vanhouter (14-0, 11 KOs) will face Belgium's Michael Essomba (11-2, 10 KOs) in another heavyweight contest.

Boxing great Manny Pacquiao and Cardiff's former world champion Joe Cordina had both been linked with appearances on the undercard, although Pacquiao is no longer expected to feature.

It remains unclear whether any further bouts will be added to the event.

The two prime ministers exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service

Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.

The contrast between the two leaders was striking.

Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.

Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.

Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.

For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.

The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.

India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.

According to Nepal's estimates, the cost of rebuilding the region hit by a devastating flash flood in September could amount to $4.8bn

The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones.

The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan".

Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.

While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy.

Although the joint statement acknowledged outstanding issues, the two leaders did not mention the border dispute in their public remarks

A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.

Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old.

His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.

According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs.

"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."

Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".

There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit.

As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity.

The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita.

There was, however, disappointment on aviation.

Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.

Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects.

"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat.

India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional.

"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough."

Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.

For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

Watch: The BBC's Katya Adler speaks to protesters taking part in recent demonstrations

France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.

This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.

President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.

That's quite a claim – and one that needs examining.

The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.

So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?

It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.

My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.

You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.

The BBC's Katya Adler talking to a protester

French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article , external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around €207m (£175.5m).

Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.

Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.

French police pepper spraying protesters during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris earlier this month

As we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said.

Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police – they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype.

"How can you justify the violence?" I ask them.

"Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard."

"We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight."

These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.

They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.

Left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block, tend to dress in all black, wearing ski masks or balaclavas

Earlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.

I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.

They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again – would only speak if they could remain anonymous.

"Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society."

How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?

They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.

Some protesters don't support the Black Block's violence but say the state's violence is worse

French intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.

Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.

Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.

He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt.

"We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me.

"We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw."

I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?

As he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do.

"The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution.

"Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us."

When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change.

Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests.

"The Black Block isn't a single organisation," says protester Starflix

There are numerous websites and Instagram profiles, mainly hosted by left-wing organisations, offering tips for protesters and rioters, such as: keep your phone at home so police can't track you, cover your face to avoid being identified and emulate martial arts expert Bruce Lee and "be like water" - appearing and disappearing into crowds. That's advice passed on by the Hong Kong protesters eight years ago.

While not formally organising the protests or violence with these posts, could the fact groups host this information online be viewed as a kind of incitement or manipulation of youngsters whose feelings are running so high in France?

All the young rioters I spoke to insist they are not being herded or directed, but is there something bigger behind what's happening?

Ultra-left protesters spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity

It takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true?

"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within."

"Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage and not just in France. You see the same rage [in protests] in Italy, Germany, Spain. It's exploding by itself."

I ask if the anti-capitalist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party (LFI) are somehow linked to the violence. They are present at most protests, supporters handing out campaign pamphlets to the chanting crowds.

But the activist denies this, telling me Mélenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He says the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch".

Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to collapse the French government?

"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people.

"More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol."

You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left.

Limoges Town Hall, allegedly damaged by protesters, has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in

This is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month . The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on.

The 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak.

Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous.

"We were all shocked by the [town hall] fire – even as we watched it happen in front of us - but it's our duty to take action," he tells me.

"I can't leave this world to my son in the state that it's in. Look how military vehicles and brute force are used by the state against our young students.

"It's amazing the people haven't taken up arms against them. Do we need a policeman killed in order for the state to listen?"

"As a child, I was educated with French values – liberty, equality, fraternity - but when I look at the social injustice in the world now, I'm disgusted. As a father, I can't let this go on. If I have to, I would take a bullet to protect the youth of this country."

These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France.

Upcoming presidential elections offer a crossroad, with polls predicting a run-off between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon

We repeatedly approached French intelligence. They didn't want to comment. A sign perhaps of the huge sensitivity of the current situation, especially with France hurtling towards an extremely charged presidential election.

But Michel Klein, a recently retired former police commissioner, told me he didn't think the radical left posed a serious threat to the French state.

"I believe there is a will from the radical left and the anarchists to try and destroy the Republic but they obviously don't have the means to do it," he told me.

He sees no risk of civil war in France (a possibility you hear some in the country discuss these days) but he identified a rising risk of clashes between far-left and far-right groups ahead of the presidential election.

Polls currently predict a run-off in the vote between nationalist candidate Marine Le Pen and anticapitalist Mélenchon.

Far-right vigilante groups have begun appearing on the edge of protests in a number of cities across France to "protect French streets", they say.

The popular hard-left presidential candidate Mélenchon attends most demos, his supporters handing political pamphlets to the chanting crowds, but he denies any links with violence.

France is so polarised, there's little sign next year's presidential vote will calm things. This turbulent mix of left and right, social and political unrest, feels like a perfect storm.

Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?

Comedian Mark Critch played Donald Trump during Prime Minister Mark Carney's speech at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner

Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.

The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.

Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.

"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.

Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.

"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.

He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."

There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.

"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.

Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."

Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.

The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster , external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's , external support for Trump.

They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media. , external

Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.

In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.

"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

Paul Potts was managing Port Talbot's Carphone Warehouse store at the time of his audition

Britain's Got Talent winner Paul Potts said he nearly missed his life-changing audition on the show because he had been unable to get time off from his job managing a phone shop.

The tenor shot to fame in 2007 after performing Nessun Dorma on the ITV talent show, but had unsuccessfully tried to change the date of his performance because of his shift at Port Talbot's Carphone Warehouse.

"It was only thanks to a colleague who normally didn't work Saturdays that came into cover me – otherwise I wouldn't have been there," he said.

He has since released six albums, reached the final of America's Got Talent: The Champions and inspired the Hollywood film One Chance.

"I actually almost didn't end up going," he told BBC Radio Wales' My Welsh Life.

Almost 20 years later, as he prepares for a special homecoming concert in Port Talbot, Potts said he was honoured to be "still doing what I love doing".

"The only reason why I'm still doing that is because people still support me and I'll always be forever grateful for that."

Potts's homecoming, marking 20 years since his victory on Britain's Got Talent, will be in the newly refurbished Princess Royal Theatre, now renamed Y Storfa.

Having seen photographs of the renovation, he said it looked like a "massive improvement", adding that investment in cultural venues was part of a wider regeneration of Port Talbot.

"It's good to see more culture coming in," he said.

He described the people in Port Talbot as a big part of what made the town special, and its community spirit appealed to him.

"I've always loved Port Talbot," he said.

"People have always been really self-deprecating and that suits my sense of being very well as well."
