Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024

A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.

Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.

Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.

This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.

In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.

At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.

On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.

"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.

"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."

Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.

Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.

According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.

Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

Ibiganiro byabo byagarutse ku ntambwe u Rwanda na Zimbabwe bimaze gutera mu guteza imbere umubano w’ibihugu byombi, ugaragarira mu masezerano y’ubufatanye yasinywe, gusurana kw’abayobozi bakuru ndetse no kungurana ubumenyi n’ubunararibonye.

Kwakira Prof. Charity Manyeruke mu biro bya Perezida, byabaye umwanya mwiza wo kureba aho ubufatanye bw’ibihugu byombi bugeze no gushimangira ko imikoranire ishingiye ku nyungu rusange igomba gukomeza no mu gihe habaye impinduka mu bahagarariye ibihugu mu butumwa bwa dipolomasi.

Umubano w’u Rwanda na Zimbabwe umaze imyaka myinshi ushingiye ku bufatanye bwa dipolomasi, ubucuruzi, uburezi, umutekano, ingufu n’iterambere ry’abaturage.

Intambwe ikomeye muri uwo mubano yatewe ku wa 6 Kanama 2025, ubwo ibihugu byombi byasinyaga amasezerano atanu y’ubufatanye mu nama ya gatatu ya Komisiyo ihuriweho ishinzwe ubufatanye (Joint Permanent Commission on Cooperation – JPCC), yabereye i Kigali.

Ayo masezerano areba ubufatanye mu nzego z’ubuzima, urubyiruko, ubufatanye hagati ya Polisi z’ibihugu byombi, guhererekanya amakuru ya gasutamo ndetse n’ingufu.

Icyo gihe Minisitiri w’Ububanyi n’Amahanga n’Ubutwererane w’u Rwanda, Olivier Jean Patrick Nduhungirehe, yavuze ko ayo masezerano agamije guhindura ubushuti n’ubufatanye bw’ibihugu byombi ibikorwa bifatika bifitiye abaturage akamaro.

Uburezi ni rumwe mu nzego zigaragaramo cyane ubufatanye bw’ibihugu byombi, by’umwihariko mu gusangira abarimu, ubumenyi n’ubunararibonye.

Mu masezerano y’ubufatanye mu burezi, Zimbabwe yohereje mu Rwanda inzobere mu burezi n’abarimu bagiye gufasha mu mashuri nderabarezi, ay'imyuga n'ayandi mashuri.

Kugeza mu mpera za 2025, Zimbabwe yari imaze kohereza mu Rwanda abakozi b’inzobere mu burezi 297, barimo icyiciro cya mbere cyageze mu 2022 n'ikindi cyageze mu 2025.

Uruhare rw’abo barimu rwagaragaye cyane mu kongerera abanyeshuri ubushobozi mu rurimi rw’Icyongereza, ubumenyi mu bumenyi n’ikoranabuhanga ndetse no guteza imbere ireme ry’uburezi.

Ku wa 19 Ugushyingo 2026, Minisitiri w’Uburezi, Dr. Joseph Nsengimana, na we yakiriye Ambasaderi Charity Manyeruke mu ruzinduko rwo kumusezeraho, baganira ku bufatanye mu burezi, by’umwihariko mu mashuri nderabarezi no gusangira ubumenyi bw’abarimu.

Umubano w’u Rwanda na Zimbabwe wagiye urushaho gukomera binyuze mu gusurana kw’abayobozi bakuru.

Muri Nzeri 2022, Perezida wa Zimbabwe, Emmerson Mnangagwa, yasuye u Rwanda aho yitabiriye inama ya Africa Green Revolution Forum.

Muri Mata 2023, Perezida Paul Kagame na we yagiye muri Zimbabwe, aho yitabiriye inama ya Transform Africa Summit yabereye i Victoria Falls.

Izi ngendo zagaragaje ubushake bw’abakuru b’ibihugu byombi bwo gukomeza guteza imbere imikoranire, haba mu nzego za politiki, ubukungu n’iterambere ry’Afurika.

Ku bijyanye n’ubucuruzi n’ishoramari, ibihugu byombi byagiye bishishikariza abikorera gushaka amahirwe yo gukorana, kongera ubucuruzi no gushora imari mu masoko ya buri gihugu.

Mu biganiro byabaye muri Kanama 2025, Minisitiri w’Ububanyi n’Amahanga wa Zimbabwe, Prof. Amon Murwira, yagaragaje ko hakiri amahirwe menshi yo kwagura ubucuruzi hagati y’ibihugu byombi, anavuga ko Zimbabwe yifuza kongera ibicuruzwa yohereza mu Rwanda birimo isukari n’imbuto za blueberries.

Gusoza inshingano kwa Ambasaderi Charity Manyeruke ntibivuze ko umubano w’u Rwanda na Zimbabwe uhagaze, ahubwo ni impinduka isanzwe mu mikorere ya dipolomasi, mu gihe ibihugu byombi bikomeje kwagura ubufatanye bwabyo.

Manyeruke yari amaze imyaka irenga irindwi ahagarariye Zimbabwe mu Rwanda, aho yagize uruhare mu guteza imbere umubano w’ibihugu byombi, by’umwihariko mu burezi no mu guhuza inzego zitandukanye.

Mu Kwakira 2026, Guverinoma y’u Rwanda yemeje Helliate Rushwaya nk'uzahagararira Zimbabwe mu Rwanda, asimbuye Charity Manyeruke.

Muri rusange, ibiganiro bya Perezida Kagame na Ambasaderi Manyeruke bibaye mu gihe u Rwanda na Zimbabwe bikomeje gushimangira umubano ushingiye ku masezerano, gusurana kw’abayobozi, gusangira ubumenyi no gushaka amahirwe mashya y’ubufatanye mu nzego zitandukanye.

Icyo ibihugu byombi bihuriyeho ni ubushake bwo guhindura ubwo mubano ibikorwa bifatika bizamura ubukungu, imibereho y’abaturage n’iterambere ry’Afurika.

Perezida wa Repubulika, Paul Kagame, yakiriye Umuyobozi uhagarariye Ishami ry’Umuryango w’Abibumbye ryita ku Iterambere (UNDP) mu Rwanda, Fatmata Lovetta Sesay, uri gusoza inshingano, baganira ku ruhare uru rwego rwagize mu gushyigikira gahunda z’iterambere ry’u Rwanda n’ibikorwa bihuriweho bizakomeza gufasha igihugu kugera ku ntego zacyo.

Ibiganiro byabo byibanze ku bufatanye hagati ya Leta y’u Rwanda na UNDP mu gushyira mu bikorwa gahunda z’ingenzi z’iterambere, zirimo guteza imbere ubushabitsi bw’urubyiruko, guhanga imirimo no kwagura imishinga ijyanye n’ingufu zirambye.

Uruhare rwa UNDP muri izo gahunda rugaragaza uburyo ubufatanye hagati y’u Rwanda n’imiryango mpuzamahanga bushobora gufasha igihugu kubona ubumenyi, ubushobozi n'ubundi bufasha bukenewe kugira ngo intego z’iterambere zigerweho.

Sesay yari amaze igihe ahagarariye UNDP mu Rwanda, aho yafatanyije n'inzego zitandukanye mu gushyigikira gahunda zigamije guteza imbere ubukungu, kongera amahirwe y'urubyiruko no kubaka iterambere rirambye.

Kimwe mu by’ingenzi UNDP yafashijemo u Rwanda ni ugushyigikira gahunda zigamije kongerera urubyiruko ubushobozi bwo kwihangira imirimo no guteza imbere ibitekerezo byarwo mu bucuruzi.

Urugero ni gahunda ya AGUKA Youth Entrepreneurship Programme, ifasha urubyiruko rufite ibitekerezo by’imishinga kubibyaza umusaruro binyuze mu mahugurwa, ubujyanama, inkunga n'amahirwe yo kubona igishoro.

Muri Kamena 2025, urubyiruko 100 rwari rwitabiriye icyiciro cya gatatu cy’iyi gahunda rwahawe igishoro fatizo cya $3.000 kuri buri rwari rwaratoranyijwe, hagamijwe kurufasha gutangiza no kwagura ibikorwa by'ubucuruzi.

Mu nyandiko yasohoye muri Gicurasi 2026, Sesay yagaragaje ko gushora imari mu rubyiruko ari ingenzi mu guhangana n'ikibazo cy'ubushomeri, ashimangira ko urubyiruko rushobora no guhanga imirimo y'abandi aho gutegereza ko ruhabwa akazi gusa.

Ikindi gice cy'ubufatanye Perezida Kagame na Sesay bagarutseho ni uguteza imbere ingufu zirambye, imwe mu nkingi z'ingenzi mu iterambere ry'ubukungu no kurengera ibidukikije.

Mu mishinga iheruka, UNDP ku bufatanye n'inzego z'u Rwanda yashyigikiye gahunda yo kugeza ingufu zisukuye ku miryango yo mu Ntara y'Iburasirazuba.

Ku wa 20 Ukwakira 2026, UNDP yagejeje mu Ntara y'Iburasirazuba uburyo bwo gutekesha biogaz bwashyizwe mu ngo 937 zo mu turere twa Rwamagana, Ngoma na Gatsibo. Iyi biogaz ikorwa mu mase y'amatungo, hasigara n'ifumbire y'imborera ikoreshwa mu buhinzi.

Uyu mushinga ugamije kugabanya ikoreshwa ry'inkwi n'amakara, kurinda abaturage umwotsi wangiza ubuzima no guteza imbere ikoreshwa ry'ingufu zisubira.

Ubufatanye nk'ubu bushobora no gufasha u Rwanda kwihutisha intego zo kwagura amashanyarazi n'ingufu zisukuye, no kugabanya ingaruka z'imihindagurikire y'ikirere.

Fatmata Lovetta Sesay afite uburambe bw'imyaka irenga 20 mu bijyanye n'iterambere ry'ubukungu, imari irambye, gushyigikira ishyirwa mu bikorwa rya politiki n'imicungire y'inzego.

Mbere yo kuza mu Rwanda, yakoze mu nzego zitandukanye za UNDP no mu bihugu birimo Ghana, Gambia, Sudani y'Epfo, Ethiopia, Kenya na Uganda, ndetse anagira uruhare mu bikorwa bya UN Women mu karere ka Afurika y'Iburasirazuba n'Amajyepfo.

Raporo y'Umuryango w'Abibumbye yo mu Ugushyingo 2026 igaragaza ko Sesay yanakoze imirimo nk'Umuhuzabikorwa w'Umuryango w'Abibumbye mu Rwanda by'agateganyo, akaba yarasoje izo nshingano agiye kujya muri Guinea, aho azakomeza inshingano nk'Umuhuzabikorwa wa Loni.

U Rwanda na UNDP bimaze imyaka myinshi bifatanya mu bikorwa by'iterambere, birimo guteza imbere ubukungu, guhanga imirimo, guhangana n'imihindagurikire y'ikirere, guteza imbere uburinganire no kongera ubushobozi bw'inzego zitandukanye.

Ibiganiro bya Perezida Kagame na Sesay bigaragaza ko ubufatanye bw'u Rwanda n'ibigo mpuzamahanga by'iterambere bukomeje kugira uruhare mu gushyigikira gahunda z'igihugu, by'umwihariko izigamije guha urubyiruko amahirwe yo kwihangira imirimo no kubaka ubukungu burambye.

Kevin de Bruyne won six Premier League titles, the Champions League, two FA Cups and five League Cups during his time at Manchester City

Kevin de Bruyne says his feelings for Manchester City will "never change" even if the club are stripped of their titles after being found guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.

De Bruyne, 35, enjoyed a trophy-laden decade at Etihad Stadium, lifting 16 trophies including the Treble in 2023 before leaving on a free transfer to join Napoli in 2025.

The Belgian returns to City for the second time on Tuesday when Napoli play them in the Champions League.

De Bruyne says he has "nothing but affection" for the club and that "will never change" even if City were forced to give up their domestic titles.

"Of course, it's a lot of things that's been going on but I cannot change anything about that. I am proud of what I have done as a football player and, honestly, this is my club," he said.

"I love the owners, I have talked about a lot of stuff outside football - I have even spoken to [chairman] Khaldoon [Al Mubarak] about how to buy a club."

City deny any wrongdoing and are appealing the decision.

In September it was revealed that an independent commission found that City had arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

How does Maresca fix City's midfield conundrum?

City await any sanctions that may be imposed following their guilty verdict, with possible punishments ranging from a hefty fine, points deductions, relegation from the Premier League and being stripped of titles.

Asserting its innocence, City said it had filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions" on 2 October.

Sources have told BBC Sport that City were expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Criticism of City has been intense, but De Bruyne said he can't "change anything" about people calling his former club a "disgrace".

"Of course, in life there are rules, but everybody plays on the limit, I would say, and for me, I played in between the white lines," he said.

"I don't think a lot of people will change in their mind how they view me as a player, or how we played, but everybody has their own opinion."

De Bruyne will be afforded a generous ovation when he returns to Etihad Stadium, having played more than 400 games for City, scoring 108 goals.

After his final home game for the club in May 2025, it was announced that a statue will be built in his honour outside the stadium.

Anchored up in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi , co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?

The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.

Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes , has called it "a dangerous escalation".

It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.

Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.

It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

How Ukraine drone attacks on Russian ships unfolded

Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.

If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?

As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.

On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders , just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.

This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.

It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders are becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.

But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.

Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile

Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.

In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.

The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.

There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.

Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.

Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.

It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.

This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.

There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

COPENHAGEN – Rwanda and Denmark have signed an agreement intended to make it easier for spouses and eligible family members of diplomats serving in either country to take up employment.

The Memorandum of Understanding on Gainful Employment for Members of Diplomatic Missions was among three bilateral instruments signed by Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, and Denmark’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, during a visit to Copenhagen.

The signing followed a bilateral meeting between the two ministers, during which they discussed strengthening relations and expanding cooperation in areas of mutual interest.

Their discussions covered shared priorities, opportunities to deepen political and economic ties, and collaboration at bilateral and multilateral levels.

Arrangements of this kind allow eligible family members accompanying diplomats to seek employment in the host country, subject to agreed procedures and national laws.

Without such arrangements, spouses and other key family members of diplomats can face restrictions that prevent them from working while accompanying their partners on foreign postings.

The agreement could therefore give Rwandan diplomats serving in Denmark, and Danish diplomats posted to Rwanda, greater flexibility by allowing eligible family members to pursue professional opportunities during their stay.

This Rwanda–Denmark agreement is not unusual as a diplomatic practice. What is notable is that the two countries have formalised the arrangement between themselves.

The two countries also signed the Rwanda–Denmark Partnership Agreement, which provides a broader framework for bilateral cooperation.

The third instrument was a Declaration of Intent on negotiating an Agreement on the Avoidance of Double Taxation (DTAA).

A future double taxation agreement would establish rules to prevent certain income from being taxed in both countries. It could cover business profits, dividends, interest, royalties and employment income, among other areas.

Such a treaty could make cross-border business and investment more predictable for companies and individuals operating between Rwanda and Denmark.

However, the declaration is a commitment to begin negotiations, not a completed tax treaty. Any eventual agreement would have to go through the necessary signing and approval procedures before taking effect.

The broader partnership comes as Rwanda and Denmark are also engaged in discussions on migration management. Denmark is among five European countries negotiating with Rwanda to establish a return centre for rejected asylum seekers who cannot be sent back to their countries of origin.

Denmark has identified 120 people who could be transferred to the planned facility when operations begin, potentially in 2027. Russians, Iranians and Syrians account for 41 per cent of those initially eligible, according to figures reported by Danish media.

The proposed arrangement is separate from the three bilateral instruments signed in Copenhagen, but adds another dimension to the two countries’ engagement.

Together, the agreements signal an effort by Kigali and Copenhagen to expand relations beyond traditional diplomacy into economic cooperation, investment and practical arrangements affecting their diplomatic missions.

Rwanda’s diplomatic relations with Denmark are handled by Ambassador Dr Diane Gashumba, who is based in Stockholm, Sweden, which is also accredited to Denmark, Finland, Norway and Iceland.

Denmark, meanwhile, is represented in Rwanda by Ambassador Casper Stenger Jensen, who is based in Kigali following the opening of Denmark’s resident embassy in Rwanda in February 2026.

While Rwanda does not have a resident embassy in Copenhagen, Denmark now maintains a diplomatic mission in Kigali.

The US Department of Commerce announced on Monday that it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

Earlier this year, "serious concerns" were raised about A&E at Ysbyty Glan Clwyd

A woman who spent 48 hours desperately unwell in an emergency department corridor says bosses at Wales' biggest health board have lost interest in patients.

Jo Hughes, 72, who is in remission from cancer, spent two days in a hospital chair with Covid, pneumonia and a kidney infection.

Another patient, who has been treated at the same hospital for 30 years, said the north Wales health board Betsi Cadwaladr is "completely leaderless" and has declined "beyond redemption".

A report into the health board's culture and leadership is expected later.

Jo Hughes fears elderly patients "wouldn't stand a chance" in an A&E corridor

After her experience at Ysbyty Glan Clwyd in Denbighshire, Hughes said: "I'm not going back to that after what I've been through."

The review was commissioned by the Welsh government in the summer, after it gave Betsi Cadwaladr a "final chance" to improve following nine years in special measures.

Earlier this month, the health board's chief executive Carol Shillabeer announced she was leaving in the new year to take up an NHS role in England.

Her departure follows a string of other senior leaders who have left the organisation in recent months, including the chief operating officer and executive director of finance.

Some patients blame senior managers for repeated failures.

Hughes, from Abergele, Conwy, was admitted to A&E on her doctor's advice last month.

"I didn't know what was happening to me. I didn't know what I'd got," she said.

"I felt awful. The best way I can describe it - it was a nightmare that I'd like to forget."

As the hours and days passed, she described "looking round to see if there was something spare that you could lie on".

She said: "I think it's the higher-ups. It's not the people on the ground, it's the chief executives, it's the bosses in my opinion. They're not doing their jobs."

Hughes said frontline staff were doing their best, but "the top people have lost interest".

The experience frightened her so much, she said she would refuse to go back to A&E.

"I would, honestly. I would say 'I'm not going, give me something here and now….I'm not going back to that after what I've been through'."

She also fears for older patients who might face the same experience, adding: "They wouldn't stand a chance.

"How could you have an 80 or 90-year-old sitting in a chair for 48 hours? It's ridiculous. No blankets, nothing like that. You're just plonked."

Patient John Cooke believes the health board is "completely leaderless"

John Cooke, 78, a retired assistant chief constable with North Wales Police, was diagnosed with Crohn's disease in 1995, and was first hospitalised with it in 1996.

Regular flare-ups mean he has been admitted to Ysbyty Glan Clwyd two to three times every year over the past three decades. While he says frontline staff continue to do their best, conditions had deteriorated overall.

"I suppose the most obvious thing is the time it takes to be seen, and certainly the time it takes to be allocated to a ward and to a bed," he said.

"When I first started on this road I could certainly be in a ward, in a bed within an hour. Now, more recently, it can be very lengthy waits, despite the pain, and I recently had a 47-hour wait in A&E before I was even seen by a doctor.

"I know of people who have waited almost a week to be allocated a bed, and very seriously ill people are not exempt from these waits at all."

He was once guaranteed quarterly outpatient appointments, but said "the treatment I'm getting now as an outpatient is almost non-existent".

Cooke says he does not believe things will improve without a "complete restructuring of the organisation".

"I blame the management. Not necessarily the board because they don't have direct access to the workforce... but the management, the senior management, the executives, they are to blame. It's completely leaderless."

He said frontline staff "work so hard and continue to labour under these conditions".

Janelt scores stunner as Brentford beat 10-man Everton

It had been some run for Everton captain James Tarkowski.

Prior to Monday night, the defender had received 74 yellow cards in the Premier League but had never been sent off - a top-flight record.

But that run came to an end at Brentford as he was given his first red card in his 351st Premier League appearance, although the decision has attracted plenty of debate.

His dismissal crucially means he will miss Sunday's Merseyside derby and also ruined David Moyes' record-breaking night as he took charge of his 593rd game as Everton boss - more than anyone else in the club's history.

The 4-0 loss was also the heaviest defeat Everton have had since Moyes returned to the club at the start of last year.

Tarkowski's dismissal proved a big talking point during and after the match, with opinions split on whether he should have gone. Even Moyes wasn't sure.

He told BBC Match of the Day: "My thoughts at the time, I didn't think it was but when I've looked at it again I think his foot high. Is there enough force for it to be a red card? Not sure about that."

James Tarkowski received his first Premier League red card

Just 15 minutes after Keane Lewis-Potter scored his second deflected strike of the evening, Everton skipper Tarkowski thundered into a challenge on Brentford 's Yehor Yarmoliuk.

He won the ball but also followed through with the challenge forcefully. Initially, referee Craig Pawson deemed a foul and a yellow card was enough.

But, after an intervention from the video assistant referee (VAR) and studying the replay, Pawson changed the yellow for a red.

The Premier League match centre said on X: "After VAR review, the referee overturned the original decision of yellow card for Tarkowski for the challenge on Yarmoliuk and issued a red card for serious foul play.

"VAR: 'Point of contact is on the shin. He's got speed and intensity. Studs are high.'

"REF: 'After review, Everton No.6 commits a challenge that endangers his opponent's safety, making contact with the studs onto the shin. Cancelling the yellow card - and a red card.'"

Referees are asked to take into account several considerations for what counts as serious foul play including the speed of the challenge, its intensity, force and what degree of control there was.

But, as always, there was plenty of debate about whether it was the correct decision.

BBC Sport's football issues correspondent Dale Johnson, said: "Really not sure about this as a VAR red card.

"Yes, Tarkowski absolutely ticks the boxes for speed and intensity and leading high with studs showing.

"But the question marks are that Tarkowski made only small contact and didn't have a straight leg when he did so.

"Maybe his reputation played a part? Remember, he wrongly escaped a VAR red card against Liverpool for a challenge, which was along the same lines. He won the ball and then followed through into Alexis Mac Allister. Thought that was a far stronger challenge."

BBC Radio 5 Live's - and former Blackburn Rovers striker - Chris Sutton, said on X: "Come on that's not a red… the game's gone."

Former Arsenal striker Alan Smith agreed the decision was harsh. He told Sky Sports: "Ten years ago we wouldn't have looked at it once and now we still [frame] it on the follow-through. I just can't see it.

"Only Tarkowski knows if he wanted to leave it high or if it was natural. The follow-through was just natural momentum.

"There's a bit of anger in there from Tarkowski and it's a little high but only he knows if he wanted to leave a little more on Yarmoliuk there."

Opinion was far from unanimous though, with both pundits in the Sky Sports studio adamant it was a clear red.

Former Liverpool centre-back Jamie Carragher said: "It's a red card. Tarkowski has got previous for tackles like that. He is a 90s defender, he tackles like that.

"He follows through with such force, it is excessive. You want to give him the benefit of the doubt but it's a red card."

He added: "You could argue was it a big enough mistake for VAR to get involved but I think we are splitting hairs. He doesn't need to do this."

While ex-Totenham defender Toby Alderweireld added: "It's a red card, he knows what he is doing. 100%."

Rangers host Aberdeen in one of two Scottish Premiership games on Tuesday

One between two sides looking to recover from embarrassing home defeats, another a match-up between two teams looking to build on decent away victories.

All four looking to make their game in hand count in Tuesday's Scottish Premiership double-header.

So what's to look out for as second-top Rangers host Aberdeen and second-bottom Hibernian entertain Dundee?

I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide - Pressley

Hibs boss Reedijk rejects talk of Easter Road jinx

Rangers plan January exit for Cifuentes - gossip

Just over a fortnight ago, a Rangers win over Aberdeen at Ibrox on Tuesday would have seemed a surefire bet.

The Dons went into the international break on the back of a 4-0 thumping at home to a Hibernian side whose victory lifted them above their hosts and left Stephen Robinson's side sitting in second-bottom place.

With his team only two points clear of bottom-placed Kilmarnock, and with the fans having failed to take the Northern Irishman to their heart, the Dons acted immediately to end his eight-month spell in charge.

They acted similarly swiftly to appoint former Luzern head coach Mario Frick as the new man in charge and his promise of "heavy metal football" immediately got a tune out of his players as they blew away Kilmarnock at Rugby Park to end a dismal run of four straight defeats.

Whether or not it was merely the traditional "new manager bounce", only time will tell, but they will certainly be heading to Glasgow with more of a spring in their step after a win that moved them up to eighth.

Given Rangers' two victories over Aberdeen this season, once in the league at Pittodrie and most recently in the League Cup semi-final at Hampden, have been by a single goal, will that renewed confidence and belief from that 4-2 win in Ayrshire be enough to tip the balance of power?

Certainly, everything else points to a home win.

In recent times, Rangers have had a tendency to pass up chances to put pressure on Celtic - and this time a win would take them to within a point of the leaders and reigning champions.

However, Saturday's late winner away to Motherwell suggests the team that Derek McInnes has built is of more sturdy stuff.

That 2-1 win at Fir Park leaves them unbeaten in 13 matches and they are also eight unbeaten at home, having won seven in a row at Ibrox by an aggregate score of 18-2.

McInnes recognises Rangers have yet to dominate games the way he would like, but at least they now appear to have found a way to create the chances that were lacking early in his tenure.

Indeed, Rangers have now scored in every one of their last 27 games in the Premiership and at Fir Park conjured up 29 goal attempts - their highest total in a single league match this season.

To put a spanner in that increasingly well-oiled machine, the Dons will have to end a run of five straight defeats, by an aggregate of 16-2, at Ibrox since their last win there in September 2023.

Overall, they have lost their latest six meetings with the Ibrox side and, to make matters worse, McInnes has won all six of his Premiership home games against Aberdeen since leaving their manager's office, four with Kilmarnock and twice with Heart of Midlothian last season.

Hibs were unable to back-up that aforementioned 4-0 win at Pittodrie as they suffered an identical home hammering against Dundee United on Saturday.

Recently appointed head coach Marink Reedijk admitted he was taken by surprise by what he said was his side's inability to do the "brilliant basics" as he calls them.

A failure to win at home will not have come as a shock to Hibs fans considering they have watched them seven times in a row now at Easter Road without being able to celebrate a victory.

However, this third straight home defeat came on the back of a three-game unbeaten run away from Leith, including that League Cup semi-final derby win over Hearts.

Reedijk refused to concede that Hibs were suffering a home jinx, but he might reconsider if his side falter again on Tuesday considering visitors Dundee are reeling from an even more painful home battering.

Hearts' 8-0 win was the Dark Blues' heaviest-ever top-flight defeat at home and has left head coach Steven Pressley admitting that "at times, I've wanted to crawl under a rock and hide".

While the former Scotland centre-half preferred to shoulder the blame for letting a bit of complacency develop, he echoed his Dutch counterpart by stressing that his side paid for not doing the basics.

In his case, that meant an admission that his squad have a fragile mentality and are not good enough to compete without working their wee cotton socks off.

Pressley is big on psychology, but how will his squad respond to such a public confession at a time when they are visiting a ground where they have not won in 20 visits since October 2001 under Ivano Bonetti?

Indeed, while Dundee are four places and six points above Tuesday's hosts, they have currently lost five of their last seven games on the road and, with Hibs having won 2-1 in the reverse fixture at Dens Park in August, are without a win in five meetings with the Edinburgh side.

To change that sorry trend and continue Hibs' home jinx, they will have to improve on Saturday's statistic of failing to even conjure up an attempt on target.

A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia

Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company had come under pressure from Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to reverse course and bring Huang back.

But Democrats have accused the Trump administration of selling out national security for financial gain. Huang is due to testify before Congress in early December.

His comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that had left the S&P 500 in correction territory.

Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value.

But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price.

Watch: Nvidia's stock skyrockets after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO

Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO.

Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns

Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire

US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal

In a brief interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to bring back Huang. Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating the CEO.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.

The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.

The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang

How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?

The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.

Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years".

"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says.

Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.

"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," Republican congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska said.

"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."

Sen Tom Cotton, fellow Republican who represents Arkansas, vowed that Congress would investigate.

"The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," he said.

Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress from January, have already promised to launch Nvidia investigations.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".

Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a member of the House foreign affairs committee, also condemned the move in a statement to the BBC as "premature" before multiple investigations are concluded. Fellow Democratic Representative Andre Carson, a member of the House intelligence committee, told the BBC that "Congress needs a full accounting of whether any controlled technology was diverted" to China.

Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December.

Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee.

Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.

The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.

Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.

Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.

The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

Gisèle Pelicot said she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay

Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.

The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.

The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."

"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.

The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.

French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.

In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.

"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.

Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.

French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".

"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.

Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".

Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.

Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.

Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.

More than a million people were forced to flee the violence across the border to Bangladesh in 2017

The UK has sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that the country had carried out genocide against the Rohingya minority – marking the first time a state has been found guilty of the crime .

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma.

The UK is joined by several other countries , external in acknowledging the ICJ ruling, including Australia, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and Canada.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values and must be matched by clear action."

Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications

The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.

Miliband added that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing , who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" as he was head of the military at the time of the genocide in 2017.

He said: "Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again."

Miliband also called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement".

The foreign secretary confirmed that new legislation would be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.

Last week, he expelled Myanmar's defence attaché after the ICJ ruled the country had committed genocide during the brutal military campaign in 2017.

He told MPs on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention , external .

In its ruling last week, the court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal. Myanmar denied the claims against it.

Reports said that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.

Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.

Myanmar's leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi , was deposed by the military in 2021.

MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan army were still happening.

Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy.

The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable.

Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines.

While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.

Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

It is now one the most valuable firms in the world and its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on it, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Some suggested his departure, which was sparked by the emergence that Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China, posed a risk to the wider AI industry.

That was because it was unclear whether Nvidia would change strategy and potentially rein in spending - a move could have had wider implications for the US economy, but which looks unlikely now Huang has returned.

The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well as being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?

That risk was perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, had called for Huang's reinstatement.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, and backed a campaign, along with shareholders and supporters, to "Bring Jensen Back".

Kathleen Brooks, research director at investment platform XTB, said Huang's return suggested he was "the godfather" of AI and has the status to shift "the dial for corporate finance".

"Is Jensen Huang the most valuable man on the planet? His return suggests more of the same when it comes to circular financing and the rapid AI infrastructure build out, and the market loves it," she added.

However, Huang's return to Nvidia does not solve the wider issues rattling the tech stock markets in recent weeks.

Investors had taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.

Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.

However, investment in AI is still expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.

The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.

President Donald Trump hailed Huang as a "great patriot and national treasure" after his reappointment and pointed to the chief executive's wider impact.

"The country needs Jensen's leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy," he wrote on Truth Social.

Nvidia said its leadership had received input from "senior levels of the United States government and was "confident that Mr Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk".
